questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four components of nodal delay d_nodal?
choices: Processing delay
Queueing delay
Retransmission delay
Propagation delay
questions.explain: d_nodal = d_proc + d_queue + d_trans + d_prop. The fourth component is transmission delay. Retransmission is not one of them.

questions.q: Which of these are part of a router's nodal processing delay (d_proc)?
choices: Checking the packet for bit errors
Looking up the forwarding table to determine the output link
Waiting in the output buffer while packets ahead of it are sent
Pushing the packet's bits onto the outgoing link
questions.explain: Processing covers integrity (bit-error) checks and deciding the output link. Waiting in the buffer is queueing delay, and pushing bits onto the link is transmission delay.

questions.q: What is the typical order of magnitude of nodal processing delay at a router?
choices: Microseconds or less
Tens of milliseconds
Hundreds of milliseconds
Several seconds
questions.explain: Forwarding lookups and integrity checks typically take microseconds or less.

questions.q: Which delay component depends most directly on the congestion level at the router's output link?
choices: Processing delay
Queueing delay
Transmission delay
Propagation delay
questions.explain: Queueing delay is the time spent waiting at the output link for transmission. It depends on how many packets are already waiting, which is the router's congestion level.

questions.q: A packet waits in a router's output buffer while packets that arrived before it are transmitted. Name this component of delay.
questions.explain: This is queueing delay (d_queue): time spent waiting at the output link for transmission.

questions.q: A 1,500-byte packet goes out a 100 Mbps link that is 2,000 km long (propagation speed 2x10^8 m/s). It waits 3 ms in the queue, and processing delay is negligible. What is the total nodal delay d_nodal, in milliseconds?
With L = packet length (bits) and R = link transmission rate (bps), the transmission delay is:
choices: d/s
L/R
L·a/R
R/L
questions.explain: d_trans = L/R, the time to push all L bits of the packet onto the link.

questions.q: With d = length of the physical link and s = propagation speed, the propagation delay is:
choices: d/s
s/d
L/R
d·s
questions.explain: d_prop = d/s, the time for a bit to travel from one end of the link to the other. s is about 2x10^8 m/s.

questions.q: How long does it take to transmit an 8,000-bit packet onto a 1 Mbps link? Give the answer in milliseconds.
What is the propagation delay over a 4,000 km link if signals propagate at 2x10^8 m/s? Give the answer in milliseconds.
Doubling a link's transmission rate R cuts its propagation delay in half.
questions.explain: Propagation delay is d/s and depends only on the link's length and the medium. Raising R reduces transmission delay (L/R), not propagation delay.

questions.q: A link is upgraded from 10 Mbps to 1 Gbps using the same cable over the same distance. Which delay stays the same?
choices: Transmission delay
Propagation delay
Neither: both change
Both: neither changes
questions.explain: Propagation delay (d/s) depends on distance and medium, which haven't changed. Transmission delay (L/R) drops because R went up.

questions.q: A 10,000-bit packet is sent on a 1 Mbps link that is 200 km long (s = 2x10^8 m/s). At the moment the last bit leaves the sender, which is true?
choices: The first bit has already reached the receiver
The first bit is still propagating along the link
The whole packet has already been received
No bits have reached the link yet
questions.explain: d_trans = 10,000/10^6 = 10 ms and d_prop = 2x10^5/2x10^8 = 1 ms. The first bit arrives after 1 ms, long before the last bit leaves at 10 ms. The last bit still needs another 1 ms to arrive.

questions.q: Transmission delay is the time it takes a single bit to travel from one end of a link to the other.
questions.explain: That describes propagation delay (d/s). Transmission delay (L/R) is the time to push all of the packet's bits onto the link.

questions.q: It takes roughly 30 ms for a signal to cross a transatlantic link from the US east coast to Europe. Which delay component is this?
choices: Processing delay
Queueing delay
Transmission delay
Propagation delay
questions.explain: Bits travel near the speed of light, but over thousands of kilometers the propagation delay (d/s) becomes noticeable. A geosynchronous satellite hop is about 270 ms.

questions.q: In the caravan analogy for packet delay, what does a single car represent?
choices: A bit
A packet
A router
A link
questions.explain: Car = bit, caravan = packet, and servicing a car at the toll booth = transmitting a bit onto the link.

questions.q: In the caravan analogy, the toll booth servicing a car corresponds to:
choices: Propagation along the link
Transmitting a bit onto the link
Waiting in a router buffer
Looking up the forwarding table
questions.explain: Toll service time is the per-bit transmission time. Driving between booths is propagation.

questions.q: A 10-car caravan reaches a toll booth that takes 12 s to service each car. Cars drive at 100 km/h, and the next toll booth is 100 km away. How many minutes until the whole caravan is lined up before the second booth?
questions.explain: Transmission: 10 x 12 s = 120 s = 2 min. Propagation of the last car: 100 km / (100 km/h) = 60 min. Total = 62 min.

questions.q: A 10-car caravan reaches a toll booth that takes 6 s to service each car. Cars drive at 100 km/h, and the next toll booth is 50 km away. How many minutes until the whole caravan is lined up before the second booth?
questions.explain: Transmission: 10 x 6 s = 60 s = 1 min. Propagation of the last car: 50 km / (100 km/h) = 0.5 h = 30 min. Total = 31 min.

questions.q: A 10-car caravan reaches a toll booth that takes 1 minute to service each car. Cars now drive at 1000 km/h, and the next booth is 100 km away. When the first car arrives at the second booth, how many cars are still at the first booth?
questions.explain: The first car finishes service at 1 min and drives 100 km / (1000 km/h) = 6 min, so it arrives at 7 min. By then 7 cars have been serviced, leaving 3 at the first booth. Bits of a packet can reach the next router while later bits are still being transmitted.

questions.q: In the classic answer of 62 minutes (10 cars, 12 s per car, 100 km at 100 km/h), how much of the total is propagation delay?
choices: 2 minutes
12 minutes
60 minutes
62 minutes
questions.explain: The last car needs 100 km / (100 km/h) = 60 min to propagate. The remaining 2 min (120 s) is transmission.

questions.q: The first car of a caravan can never reach the second booth while other cars of the same caravan are still waiting at the first booth.
questions.explain: If propagation is fast relative to service time (e.g., 1 min per car at 1000 km/h over 100 km), the first car arrives after 7 min while 3 cars are still at the first booth.

questions.q: With a = average packet arrival rate, L = packet length (bits), and R = link bandwidth (bps), traffic intensity is:
choices: La/R
R/(La)
L/R
a/R
questions.explain: Traffic intensity = La/R = (arrival rate of bits) / (service rate of bits).

questions.q: In the traffic intensity expression La/R, what does a stand for?
choices: Link bandwidth in bits per second
Average packet arrival rate
Packet length in bits
Propagation speed of the medium
questions.explain: a is the average packet arrival rate (packets/s), so La is the arrival rate in bits/s.

questions.q: Packets of 1,000 bits arrive at a router's output link at an average of 800 packets/s. The link rate is 1 Mbps. What is the traffic intensity?
What happens to the average queueing delay when traffic intensity La/R is greater than 1?
choices: It is small, because the link is fully used
It levels off at a fixed maximum value
It grows without bound (average delay is infinite)
It drops to zero
questions.explain: When La/R > 1, more work arrives than the link can serve. The backlog keeps growing, so the average delay is infinite.

questions.q: How does average queueing delay behave as traffic intensity La/R approaches 1 from below?
choices: It increases slowly and linearly
It becomes very large very quickly
It stays roughly constant
It decreases
questions.explain: The delay curve is nearly flat at low intensity and shoots upward as La/R nears 1, like traffic jams on a highway near capacity.

questions.q: Which changes would lower the traffic intensity La/R on a router's output link?
choices: Increase the link transmission rate R
Decrease the average packet arrival rate a
Send shorter packets (smaller L)
Shorten the physical length of the link
questions.explain: Traffic intensity depends only on L, a and R. The link's physical length affects propagation delay, not traffic intensity.

questions.q: An output link runs at 12 Mbps and all packets are 1,500 bytes. What is the largest average arrival rate a, in packets per second, that keeps traffic intensity at or below 1?
When traffic intensity is close to 0, an arriving packet usually finds little or no queue ahead of it, so average queueing delay is small.
questions.explain: La/R near 0 means little arriving work compared with link capacity, so a queue rarely forms.

questions.q: When does a router drop (lose) a packet due to congestion?
choices: When the packet arrives to find the buffer (queue) full
When the packet's propagation delay exceeds its transmission delay
When traffic intensity is close to 0
When processing determines the packet's output link
questions.explain: The buffer before a link has finite capacity. A packet arriving to a full queue has nowhere to be stored, so it is dropped.

questions.q: After a packet is dropped at a full router buffer, what may happen to it?
choices: It is retransmitted by the previous node
It is retransmitted by the source end system
It is not retransmitted at all
The same router restores it from the buffer once space frees up
questions.explain: A lost packet may be retransmitted by the previous node, by the source end system, or not at all. A dropped packet was never stored, so the router cannot restore it.

questions.q: Because routers buffer packets, a packet arriving at a busy output link is never dropped. It just waits longer.
questions.explain: Buffers have finite capacity. A packet that arrives while the buffer is full is dropped.

questions.q: A router's output queue grows longer when:
choices: The arrival rate to the link (temporarily) exceeds the link's capacity
The outgoing link is physically very long
Packets are shorter than usual
Processing delay is in the microseconds
questions.explain: Queues build when packets arrive faster than the output link can transmit them. If this lasts long enough, the buffer fills and losses follow.

questions.q: An output link with a finite buffer has traffic intensity well above 1 for a sustained period. What will a growing share of arriving packets experience?
choices: Being dropped (packet loss)
Lower propagation delay
Lower transmission delay
Bypassing nodal processing
questions.explain: With more work arriving than the link can serve, the finite buffer fills. Packets arriving to the full buffer are lost, and under heavy congestion loss rates can be high (10-20% of packets has been observed).

questions.q: Queueing delay and congestion-related packet loss come from the same cause: packets arriving at an output link faster than it can transmit them.
questions.explain: Arrivals that outpace transmission make the queue grow, which causes queueing delay. Once the finite buffer is full, further arrivals are dropped.

questions.q: What does the traceroute program measure?
choices: Round-trip delay from the source to each router along the path toward a destination
One-way propagation delay of each link only
The throughput of each link on the path
The buffer size at each router
questions.explain: For each hop, the sender measures the time from sending a probe until the router's reply returns. That is a round-trip time (RTT).

questions.q: How many probe packets does traceroute send toward each router (hop) on the path?
questions.explain: Traceroute sends three probes per hop, so each line of output shows three RTT measurements.

questions.q: How does traceroute make its probes stop at, and get a reply from, router i on the path?
choices: It sets the probe's time-to-live (TTL) field to i
It sends exactly i copies of the probe
It waits i milliseconds before sending
It sets the packet length to i bytes
questions.explain: Probes for router i carry a TTL of i, so they reach router i, which returns a packet to the sender.

questions.q: In traceroute output, what does a line of "* * *" mean?
choices: No response: the probes were lost or the router isn't replying
The delay was too small to measure
The destination has been reached
The router replied with the maximum possible RTT
questions.explain: A * means no reply came back for that probe, so no RTT could be measured.

questions.q: In a traceroute from gaia.cs.umass.edu (Massachusetts) to eurecom.fr (France), the RTT jumps from about 22 ms at a router in Washington, DC to about 105 ms at the next hop in Europe. What mainly explains the jump?
choices: Propagation delay across the trans-oceanic link
Processing delay at the European router
Transmission delay of the probe packets
Traceroute sending more probes to that hop
questions.explain: That hop crosses the Atlantic, and the long physical distance adds a large propagation delay.

questions.q: Traceroute sometimes shows a smaller RTT to a later (farther) router than to an earlier one. How is that possible?
choices: Queueing delays along the path change over time, and each probe is measured at a different moment
Packets travel faster the farther they go
Propagation speed increases over longer links
Traceroute subtracts processing delay for later hops
questions.explain: Congestion, and so queueing delay, changes over time. A probe to a farther router can meet less queueing than an earlier probe to a nearer router.

questions.q: Each delay value traceroute prints is the one-way delay from the source to that router.
questions.explain: Traceroute measures round-trip time: from sending the probe until the router's reply arrives back at the sender.

questions.q: Which best defines throughput?
choices: The rate (bits per unit time) at which bits are sent from sender to receiver
The time for a packet to travel from sender to receiver
The number of packets dropped per second
The transmission rate of the fastest link on the path
questions.explain: Throughput is a rate in bits/time unit. It can be instantaneous (at a point in time) or average (over a longer period).

questions.q: A download's rate goes up and down from second to second, between 1 and 9 Mbps. In total it moves 50 Mb in 10 s. What is its average throughput over that interval, in Mbps?
questions.explain: Average throughput = bits transferred / time = 50 Mb / 10 s = 5 Mbps. The second-to-second values are instantaneous throughput.

questions.q: A server sends a large file to a client over two links in series: the server's link is Rs = 2 Mbps and the client's link is Rc = 10 Mbps. What is the average end-to-end throughput, in Mbps?
questions.explain: End-to-end throughput is limited by the thinnest pipe: min(Rs, Rc) = min(2, 10) = 2 Mbps.

questions.q: What is a bottleneck link?
choices: The link on the end-to-end path that constrains end-to-end throughput
The link with the longest propagation delay
The link closest to the sending server
The link with the most packet loss in the past
questions.explain: The bottleneck is the link that limits end-to-end throughput, usually the one with the smallest transmission rate available to the flow.

questions.q: Ten server-client connections fairly share a backbone link of R = 100 Mbps. Each server's access link is Rs = 20 Mbps and each client's is Rc = 5 Mbps. What is the per-connection end-to-end throughput, in Mbps?
questions.explain: Per-connection throughput = min(Rc, Rs, R/10) = min(5, 20, 10) = 5 Mbps. The client access link is the bottleneck.

questions.q: Ten server-client connections fairly share a backbone link of R = 30 Mbps. Each server's access link is Rs = 20 Mbps and each client's is Rc = 15 Mbps. What is the per-connection end-to-end throughput, in Mbps?
questions.explain: min(Rc, Rs, R/10) = min(15, 20, 3) = 3 Mbps. The shared backbone is the bottleneck here.

questions.q: In practice, where is the bottleneck link for a server-to-client connection most often found?
choices: At the network edge: the server's or client's access link (Rs or Rc)
In the shared backbone link in the network core
On whichever link is physically longest
On the link with the most routers attached
questions.explain: Core links are usually provisioned so that R/N is larger than Rs or Rc. The access link at the edge is typically the bottleneck.

questions.q: A server sends a 40-megabit file to a client. The server's access link is Rs = 4 Mbps and the client's is Rc = 10 Mbps. Ignoring all other delays, about how many seconds does the transfer take?
questions.explain: Throughput = min(4, 10) = 4 Mbps, so time = 40 Mb / 4 Mbps = 10 s.

questions.q: A client's access link is Rc = 1 Mbps. Upgrading the server's access link from Rs = 2 Mbps to 100 Mbps will noticeably increase the end-to-end throughput to that client.
questions.explain: Throughput is min(Rs, Rc). It was already limited to 1 Mbps by the client's link, and upgrading the server side doesn't change that bottleneck.
